title: Dizi
subtitle: Iranian lamb and chickpea pot
excerpt: Dizi is the stone-pot name for the ancient Persian lamb and chickpea broth eaten in two courses: the strained broth first over bread, then the mashed solids eaten separately. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Dizi is the everyday name for abgoosht in Tehran and central Iran, named for the stone pot it is cooked in. It has been eaten in Iranian teahouses and restaurants for centuries.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze broth and mashed solids separately. Keeps well for 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before and reheat gently. The flavour deepens overnight.

glossaryTerms.definition: The stone or clay pot traditionally used to cook and serve Persian lamb broth, also the popular name for the dish itself in Tehran restaurants.
The traditional method of pouring the strained dizi broth over torn flatbread to form the first course, before eating the mashed meat and vegetables separately.

content.text: gives this broth its name. At the table, the broth is strained off and poured over torn flatbread in a deep bowl, creating what is called
. Then the solids are mashed and eaten. Three hours of slow cooking is non-negotiable. Serves 4.
Use bone-in lamb for the richest broth. The bones release collagen that gives the soup body and a glossy finish.

items.prepNote: soaked overnight in cold water, drained

content.text: Place the lamb, drained chickpeas, onion, tinned tomatoes, turmeric, cinnamon stick and water in the stockpot. Bring to a boil over high heat. Skim any foam that rises to the surface during the first 10 minutes.
Reduce to a very low simmer. Cover and cook for 2 hours. After 2 hours add the halved potatoes and the dried chilli if using. Cover and cook for a further 1 hour.
Remove the bones and cinnamon stick from the pot. Use a slotted spoon to transfer all the solid ingredients to a large bowl. The broth remains in the pot.
Serve the first course: ladle the broth into bowls over torn pieces of flatbread. This is the tirit. Eat this course first.

For the second course, pound the lamb, potato and chickpeas in the pestle and mortar to a rough paste. Add a ladle of hot broth to loosen. Serve in a bowl or on a plate with flatbread, raw sliced onion and fresh herbs.

attrs.solution: Always soak dried chickpeas for a full 12 hours. If they are still firm, cook for an additional 30 to 45 minutes. Hard water can slow chickpea cooking; adding a pinch of bicarbonate of soda to the soaking water helps.
Skim the surface during cooking and again after refrigerating overnight. Cold fat solidifies and can be lifted off easily the next day. Use the defatted broth for serving.
Add hot broth to the mash a spoonful at a time until the consistency is spreadable. The mash should be soft enough to scoop with flatbread.

content.text: Dizi restaurants are found on almost every major street in Tehran. They serve the dish in individual small stone pots that arrive at the table still simmering. Diners strain and mash their own portions at the table. It is an unhurried, social meal. The combination of lamb bones and long cooking makes dizi one of the most deeply flavoured broths in Persian cooking.
